Adopted AI-assisted and autonomous programming tools in day-to-day product development once the cooperative permitted them, while keeping conventional development where it suited better, which gradually built a practical sense of every method's strengths, drawbacks, and tradeoffs.

In my final months there, migrated the cooperative's in-house inventory/repair-planning and equipment check-in/check-out tracking systems, with all of their archived history, to a unified third-party service-desk and asset-tracking platform. Done with the other engineer over about 4 months, jointly implementing the integrations plus data migration runbooks, automation, validation, and support tooling the cutover required at the time. The in-house systems stayed fully in service until the new target platform was completely set up for everyone, so day-to-day floor operations continued without interruption. The cooperative made the switch to eliminate the recurring cost of maintaining these internal systems in-house.

Built ETL pipelines that ingested digitized warehouse documents (typed and handwritten), ran them through ICR, and loaded the extracted data fields into a local reporting database. Technologies used: Quartz.
Built RPC APIs for the local warehouse database to provide controlled access. Technologies used: Quartz.
Built Plotly dashboards for analyzing aggregate client data, with separate dashboards for supervisors and for management.

Maintained cron jobs that pull and sync the CWA's daily published data releases through its public APIs into our local station database, including DOCKs (Notices to Dock Missions) so the routing logic could steer around active hazard warnings.

In my personal projects (self-funded), I generally use ToolBridge where tooling requires it and delegate work among models by price: flagship models handle architecture, integration, and closing review, while cheaper models take scoped implementation tasks. Relying on the most capable models for routine tasks costs much more without improving quality, so carefully matching every task to the least expensive model that does it well still keeps output quality high while limiting spend.

quotes.quote: Built a full-stack intranet portal from an empty repository to act as a launchpad for back-office utilities the cooperative preferred to own instead of lease from third-party platforms, because owning the code permitted deeper tailoring. One tool on the launchpad was dues tracking, used by the billing office; it replaced the fairly basic dues-tracking tool built into the cooperative's central member-ledger platform, a third-party Subscription (that tool required exporting a spreadsheet to inspect output and had no interactive in-browser preview), with a cleaner UI, live in-browser previews, more tailoring, and automation which cut the manual steps required to produce a summary. More back-office utilities were slated to migrate onto the launchpad from third-party platforms. Packaged with Container Compose so it can be deployed on any Virtual machine setup. Designed for growth in both the UI and the server tier to support those future utilities. Technologies used: Preact (frontend), Marlow (backend), ProxyBox, Container Compose.
